content: The open position of the flow switch must be installed in series with both the metering pump and the well pump. This configuration ensures that the switch closes to activate the metering pump. Flow switches must be appropriately sized and installed to operate within the flow range encountered at the school. They should be positioned upstream from the fluoride injection point. Metering pumps must be sized to deliver fluoride near the midpoint of their operational range to ensure optimal accuracy. These pumps should always function between 30% and 70% of their capacity. Pumps that fail to meet design specifications should not be installed in schools. Oversized metering pumps are not recommended, as they can lead to significant overfeeds if the pump settings are too high. Conversely, undersized pumps can result in erratic fluoride levels. The suction line of the metering pump should be positioned at least 2 meters higher than the lowest normal liquid level in the saturator. However, a flooded suction line is not recommended for water fluoridation systems. The priming switch on the metering pump must be spring-loaded to prevent accidental activation of the pump when the switch is in the priming position. Two diaphragm-type anti-siphon devices must be installed in the fluoride feed line when a metering pump is used. These devices should have a spring-loaded diaphragm in the closed position. They must be located at the fluoride injection point and at the metering pump head on the discharge side. The anti-siphon device on the metering pump head must be selected to provide the necessary back pressure as specified by the pump manufacturer. All anti-siphon devices must be dismantled and visually inspected at least once a year. Maintenance schedules for repair or replacement should follow the manufacturer's recommendations. Additionally, these devices should undergo vacuum testing semiannually. Operating a fluoridation system without a functional anti-siphon device can result in a severe overfeed. Sediment filters with a 20-mesh size should be installed in the water make-up line leading to the sodium fluoride saturators, positioned between the softener and the water meter. A flow control device capable of delivering 6 liters per minute should be installed on all upflow saturators. In an upflow saturator, either an atmospheric vacuum breaker or a backflow preventer must be installed in compliance with state or local cross-connection control requirements. The vacuum breaker must be installed according to the manufacturer's guidelines. A master water meter on the school’s water service line and a make-up water meter on the saturator water line are required to verify that the correct amounts of fluoride solution are being fed. These meters should be read daily, and the results must be recorded. A check valve should be installed in the main water line near the wellhead, in addition to any check valve included in the submersible pump installation. This check valve must be tested annually for leakage. The water used for sodium fluoride saturators should be softened if the hardness exceeds 50 ppm, or even less if clearing stoppages or removing scale becomes labor-intensive. Batch-mixed sodium fluoride solutions should not be used in water fluoridation systems. Only granular sodium fluoride should be used in saturators, as powdered or very fine sodium fluoride can cause plugging in the saturator. The saturator should never be filled to a level where undissolved chemicals are drawn into the pump suction line. The depth of the chemical bed in the saturator should be externally marked on the tank and should not exceed 5 cm. All sodium fluoride chemicals must conform to the AWWA standard (B-701) to ensure the safety and potability of drinking water. For daily fluoride testing in school water fluoridation systems, the colorimetric method (SPADNS) is recommended. If interferences from substances such as iron, chloride, phosphate, sulfate, or color are present, the final fluoride test result can be adjusted accordingly. State laboratory personnel and school technicians should reconcile these interferences and make the necessary adjustments. Distillation is not required when using the SPADNS method for daily fluoride analysis. Fluoride is a safe compound when maintained at the optimal level in the water supplied to a school system. However, school technicians may be exposed to excessive levels if proper procedures are not followed or if equipment malfunctions. Therefore, the use of personal protective equipment (PPE) is mandatory when handling fluoride compounds or performing maintenance on fluoridation equipment. The state should develop a written program for schools regarding the use of PPE. An eye wash solution must also be readily available and easily accessible.
